q: Calculate the percentage decrease in alveolar surface area in emphysema.
Explain how the change in alveolar width is linked to the change in surface area.
The walls break down, so many small alveoli merge into fewer, larger spaces. Large spaces have far less surface for the same volume.
Explain why blood oxygen saturation is lower in emphysema, and why the gap is larger after walking.

Less surface means less diffusion of oxygen into the blood. During exercise the muscles need more oxygen and blood flows faster through the capillaries, so there is less time to load it: saturation falls to 84%.
Suggest why people with emphysema breathe faster at rest.
Each breath loads less oxygen, so they breathe faster to keep the concentration gradients for O₂ and CO₂ steep; rising CO₂ in the blood is detected and triggers faster breathing.
Suggest why less air is breathed out in the first second in emphysema.
The lungs lose their elastic fibres, so they recoil less and small airways collapse: air is pushed out slowly.

24.t: Working with data: lung volumes and fitness
q: Calculate the mean vital capacity of the swimmers.
Calculate the percentage difference in vital capacity between the groups.
The swimmers’ vital capacity has an SD of 0.5 dm³. Evaluate whether the two groups really differ.
The means differ by 0.8 dm³, but the SDs (0.5 and 0.6) mean the values overlap a lot, and the samples are small (12). A statistical test such as a t-test is needed before concluding.
Suggest why tidal volume at rest is the same in both groups.
At rest both groups need about the same amount of oxygen, so they breathe the same volume; tidal volume matches demand, not the maximum lung size.
A student concludes that swimming increases vital capacity. Evaluate this conclusion.

This is a correlation, not proof of cause. The swimmers are 9 cm taller, and taller people have larger lungs; people with large lungs may also choose swimming. Measuring the same people before and after training, or matching heights, would test the claim.
